CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: liver

3 of 5 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 0 fall below it; 2 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

  • Glycogen: ✓ detectable (both)
  • Mobile protein/peptide amide pool: ✓ detectable (both)
  • L-Glutamine: ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)
  • L-Glutamate: ? unknown (not simulated)
  • L-Alanine: ? unknown (not simulated)

Excluded before simulation (not stored in the tissue): [model's own exclusion] Glycosaminoglycans (gagCEST) - ABSENT as a major normal-liver CEST target; GAGs are the cartilage/disc CEST target and are only elevated in hepatic fibrosis (pathological), with no quantitative normal-liver mM value found.; [model's own exclusion] Creatine / Phosphocreatine - PMID 11665842 reports 'low in liver, kidney and lung (5-8 micromol/g wet weight)' (~2-4 mM), below a reliable >1 mM CEST threshold for liver.; [model's own exclusion] Lactate - all retrieved lactate studies (PMID 36623962, 37350743, 29509585) report arterial BLOOD lactate, not liver tissue content; excluded per tissue-storage rule.; [model's own exclusion] ATP / ADP / inorganic phosphate / PCr as 31P resonances - off-target for 1H CEST (31P-only observables).; [model's own exclusion] PME / PDE / total choline / lipid CH2 - 31P/1H MRS peak groupings of chemically unrelated compounds, not chemically defined molecules or polymers.; [model's own exclusion] Bile constituents / pancreatic juice / urine - secreted fluids, not tissue-stored; excluded per tissue-storage rule.; [model's own exclusion] Glutathione (GSH) - present in liver but retrieved abstracts (e.g. PMID 6864334) report only percent change vs control, no absolute mM tissue value; insufficient direct evidence.; [model's own exclusion] Taurine - retrieved abstracts report exogenous dosing or relative changes, no absolute normal-liver wet-tissue mM value.

Recommended field strength(s): 0.5 T, 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: robust

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (glycosyl hydroxyl OH (C2,C3,C6) [hydroxyl]: concentration 277-378 mM, kex fixed at 31850 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown); glycogen aliphatic C-H (rNOE, upfield membrane-like tail) [rnoe]: concentration 277-378 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 1.18-1.59%, 1.5 T: 1.84-2.49%, 3 T: 3.07-4.14%, 5 T: 4.47-6.00%, 7 T: 5.03-6.74%. Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis: The 1.0 ppm OH pool overlaps amide pools (3.5 ppm) and the semisolid MT pool (-2.4 ppm); separations 53-745 Hz vs combined linewidths ~5000-21000 Hz, so it blurs at all fields, worst at 0.5 T. The -1.1 ppm rNOE pool overlaps the semisolid MT pool (-2.4 ppm) at all fields (83-387 Hz vs ~16000 Hz linewidth) - the glycoNOE contrast is not cleanly separable from the MT tail.

Direct water saturation: Direct-sat bandwidth only 10.6 Hz (B1=0.25 µT all fields). At 0.5 T, +1 ppm is 21 Hz and -1.1 ppm is ~23 Hz, both near the 10.6 Hz band edge (OH pool borderline masked). At >=1.5 T both offsets clear the band comfortably.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: rNOE kex=5/s from a class-level phantom/solution value (PMID 25996515); shift -1.1 ppm is a median of MOUSE MUSCLE in-vivo values (PMID 42076810, 39529314) - no liver measurement. NOE transfer depends on tumbling/packing/field; muscle-to-liver is a genuine borrowing. Hydroxyl kex=31850/s is from in-vitro mouse glycogen solution (PMID 38933551); the perfused-mouse-liver study (PMID 25946616) found in-vivo liver glycogen CEST SMALLER than solution - i.e. effective in-vivo visibility is lower than this phantom rate. Confidence reduced on both pools.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=500 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 1.272% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=2000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Winning pool is a slow NOE-transfer relay; slow-exchange pools peak at low B1 (higher B1 broadens and drags the pool under direct water saturation). Swept optimum sits at the grid floor (0.25 µT). Contrast 1.991%.
    recommended sequence: 1.991% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Same slow-relay physics; longer Tsat to reach quasi-steady NOE transfer; B1 at grid floor. Higher B0 improves Hz separation from MT. Contrast 3.32%.
    recommended sequence: 3.320% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — B1 stays at the 0.25 µT floor; contrast rises purely from B0 widening Hz separation from the MT pool. Contrast 4.825%.
    recommended sequence: 4.825% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Best Hz separation; B1 at floor, slow-relay optimum unchanged. Contrast 5.42%.
    recommended sequence: 5.420% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: The -1.1 ppm NOE pool is upfield and overlaps semisolid MT, so a single-point MTRasym at -1.1 ppm is confounded by MT. Use multi-pool Lorentzian/QCEST (PMID 42076810) or AREX at low B1 to strip MT/direct-sat bias. For the downfield 1 ppm OH pool, MTRasym with a -1 ppm NOE reference cancels MT - what the human studies (26391991, 36161668) do. AREX preferred given the borrowed kex.

Potential clinical impact

No verified disease application of this pool's CEST/NOE signal was found. Searched glycoCEST, liver glycogen CEST, hepatic steatosis, and glycogen MRS/13C-MRS. Steatosis-specific glycoCEST returned nothing. No CEST application to a chronic disease (all CEST studies were fasting/meal or CCl4).

Caveats / critique (6 points, 296 words) — 300 mM (range 277-378 mM) is defensible only for a fed/post-prandial state. 13C MRS (PMID 32157774) shows liver glycogen drops ~80 mmol/L overnight, so a fastin…
  • 300 mM (range 277-378 mM) is defensible only for a fed/post-prandial state. 13C MRS (PMID 32157774) shows liver glycogen drops ~80 mmol/L overnight, so a fasting subject's concentration could be a large fraction below this. The simulated 300 mM is exactly what was scored, so contrast overstates a fasting liver.
  • The high-contrast pool is an upfield rNOE at -1.1 ppm (5 C-H, borrowed from mouse muscle) with a class-level phantom kex=5/s. The human-liver-validated 'glycoCEST' is DOWNFIELD at +1 ppm (the hydroxyl pool), which the chemist dismissed as weak. The chemist over-credited the unvalidated upfield NOE and under-credited the liver-validated OH feature.
  • The 13-proton rNOE group was correctly NOT simulated (not per-repeating-unit). Human liver glycoCEST in the literature is at ~1.0 ppm (MTRasym 1 ppm; integrated 0.5-1.5 ppm) - the downfield hydroxyl pool. The simulation's strongest contrast is an UPFIELD NOE at -1.1 ppm borrowed from mouse muscle (PMID 42076810).
  • No liver-validated upfield offset; the -1.1 ppm peak may not be where liver glycogen actually gives contrast. None. Amine/guanidinium absent. Hydroxyl (3 H) and C-H rNOE both accounted for; the 13-proton whole-polymer rNOE was rightly rejected as not per-repeating-unit. Groups not simulated: glycogen rNOE (C-H relay) [rnoe] -- not simulated: Glycogen: n_exchangeable_protons=13 is not a per-molecule (or per-repeating-unit) proton count.
  • Use 1-12; for a polymer or macromolecular pool give the concentration PER repeating unit (e.g. glycogen ~250-300 mM glucosyl units x 3 hydroxyl protons; the mobile-protein amide pool ~200-300 mM x 1), not a whole-molecule count. no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor
  • Values are in mmol/L of tissue water; convert to per-kilogram-dry-weight (mmol/kg) for MRS cross-tissue comparisons. Highly dynamic across the fed-fasted cycle.

Mobile protein/peptide amide pool — CEST: ✓ detectable (both)

Concentration: 200.00 mM typical (~100-500 mM of mobile amide units (order-of-magnitude estimate))

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: ESTIMATE, not a measured value. No paper gives a direct mM number for the mobile amide pool. Liver wet protein is ~180 g/L; total protein = ~1.6 M amino-acid residues. Only the small, mobile protein/peptide fraction (roughly 10-20% of total protein) contributes to the APT signal, giving a few hundred mM of mobile amide units. This is consistent with the robust APTw (3.5 ppm) signals observed in human liver.

Recommended field strength(s): 0.5 T, 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: robust

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (aliphatic side-chain C-H (rNOE) [rnoe]: concentration 100-500 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown); backbone amide NH (APT) [amide]: concentration 100-500 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.58-2.84%, 1.5 T: 0.52-8.31%, 3 T: 0.65-14.58%, 5 T: 0.91-19.40%, 7 T: 1.02-21.07%. Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • CRITICAL: the APT pool at +3.5 ppm and the L-Glutamine amide at +3.5 ppm have 0.0 Hz separation at EVERY field (combined linewidth only ~52.7 Hz) - perfectly degenerate in this run; any 3.5 ppm APT number is really all amides.
  • The -3.5 ppm rNOE overlaps the semisolid MT pool (-2.4 ppm): 23.4 Hz separation at 0.5 T vs ~16000 Hz linewidth (fully blurred); only starts to clear in Hz at 5-7 T (1256-1758 Hz) but still inside the MT linewidth.
  • APT vs 1.0 ppm OH: 159.7-745.1 Hz vs ~5111 Hz linewidth - overlaps at low field, separates in Hz by 5-7 T.

Direct water saturation: Direct-sat bandwidth 10.6 Hz at 0.5 T, 21.3-31.9 Hz at 1.5-7 T (B1 0.5-0.75 µT). The 3.5 ppm APT pool is 73.5-220.5 Hz from water - safely outside direct-sat at all fields; the -3.5 ppm rNOE likewise. No masking; the real issue is pool overlap, not water saturation.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Amide kex=65.5/s is a class-level median of two in-vivo measurements (116/s human brain PMID 40228056; 15/s in vivo PMID 23008121) with a 15-158/s spread and NO liver-specific measurement - 'borrowed from brain'. Liver pH/ionic environment can shift amide kex; the 8x spread means the in-vivo liver rate is uncertain. rNOE kex=5/s from a phantom (PMID 25996515), shift -3.5 ppm from brain - both borrowed. Confidence reduced on both pools.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 1.161% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Amide kex ~65/s is intermediate exchange; peak B1 sits just above the grid floor (0.5 µT) and the optimum B1 rises with B0 (to 0.75 µT by 3 T). At low B1 the amide saturates efficiently without dragging direct water saturation across 3.5 ppm. Contrast 2.99%.
    recommended sequence: 2.990% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Higher B0 pushes the intermediate-exchange optimum B1 up to 0.75 µT; 3 s to reach quasi-steady amide transfer. Contrast 4.409%.
    recommended sequence: 4.409% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — B1 at grid ceiling 0.75 µT; continued contrast gain is from B0 widening Hz separation from the OH pool. Contrast 6.084%.
    recommended sequence: 6.084% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Same; B1 at ceiling, benefit purely from Hz separation. Contrast 6.711%.
    recommended sequence: 6.711% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note:

  • Because APT (3.5 ppm) is frequency-degenerate with the glutamine amide and the Z-spectrum carries large upfield MT/NOE background, a single-point MTRasym at 3.5 ppm is the most robust and is what the liver literature actually uses (26334509, 26391991, 36161668) - it tolerates pool overlap and the narrow amide linewidth.
  • To separate APT from the -3.5 ppm rNOE and semisolid MT, use multi-pool Lorentzian (IDEAL/LD) or AREX at low B1 (PMID 40312958, 30058148). Omega-plot (multiple B1) gives concentration- vs kex-independent APT (PMID 36089834). Given the borrowed kex, AREX/omega-plot are preferred over bare MTRasym for quantification.

Potential clinical impact

No verified disease application of this pool's CEST/NOE signal was found. Searched APT/amide proton transfer liver, APT liver fibrosis, APT hepatocellular carcinoma. Found CEST applications in humans and mice. No independent (non-CEST) amide-pool metabolite-change study identified.

Caveats / critique (5 points, 241 words) — 200 mM (range 100-500 mM) for the mobile-protein amide pool is plausible (liver is very protein-dense, ~1 amide per residue). The wide 100-500 mM range reflects…
  • 200 mM (range 100-500 mM) for the mobile-protein amide pool is plausible (liver is very protein-dense, ~1 amide per residue). The wide 100-500 mM range reflects genuine tissue variability and is why the contrast uncertainty band is large (e.g. 3 T: 0.65-14.6%). Backbone amide NH (1 H, 3.5 ppm, class amide): class correct, canonical APT proton.
  • Aliphatic side-chain C-H (6 H, -3.5 ppm, class rnoe): correct as a dipolar NOE pool, but the -3.5 ppm shift is borrowed from brain/phantom and the 5/s rate is a class-level phantom value - no liver-specific NOE. No neglected exchangeable protons: backbone amide + aliphatic rNOE is the right protein-pool decomposition.
  • APT at 3.5 ppm is confirmed in-vivo in liver (PMID 26334509, 26391991, 36161668), matching the chemist's 3.5 ppm estimate. The -3.5 ppm aliphatic rNOE offset has no liver in-vivo confirmation - borrowed from brain/phantom. None. Backbone amide and aliphatic C-H rNOE both present; carboxylate/other side-chain groups are not distinct CEST-relevant pools for this generic pool.
  • no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor Concentration is an order-of-magnitude estimate; the APT signal also depends on mobile-fraction dynamics and B0. Immobile large proteins contribute to MT/semisolid background, not the sharp 3.5 ppm APT peak.
  • [Unsourced reasoning] 1 numeric step(s) rest on an unsourced assumption: 'Only a fraction of protein (small mobile proteins + peptides, excludin'.

L-Glutamine — CEST: ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)

Concentration: 30.00 mM typical (~20-50 mmol/L wet tissue (estimate from mmol/g dry reference tables)) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: ESTIMATE, not a measured value. PMID 4400073 shows a rapid wash-out release of intracellular glutamine (15.6+/-0.8 umol/h per g wet wt in the first 15 min) attributed to 'wash-out of preexisting intracellular glutamine', consistent with a substantial pool, but gives no absolute mM. Reference tables (Bergmeyer / Williamson & Brosnan) place liver L-glutamine at ~1-2 mmol/g dry; converting to wet basis (~70% water) gives ~20-50 mmol/L wet.

Recommended field strength(s): 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: fragile

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (side-chain primary amide NH2 [amide]: concentration 20-50 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.07-0.61%, 1.5 T: 0.20-1.71%, 3 T: 0.24-3.14%, 5 T: 0.33-4.25%, 7 T: 0.37-4.65%. Threshold 0.5%. Only the point estimate clears the threshold; the low corner does not.

Frequency-collision analysis: 0.0 Hz separation from the protein APT pool at every field (3.5 ppm vs 3.5 ppm) - the glutamine 'amide' is inseparable from APT by construction of this run; any glutamine contrast is indistinguishable from APT. Also overlaps the 1.0 ppm OH pool (53-745 Hz vs ~5111 Hz linewidth) at low field, improving in Hz at high field. The degeneracy is an artifact of forcing the primary amide to the backbone-amide shift.

Direct water saturation: Direct-sat bandwidth 21.3-31.9 Hz (B1 0.5-0.75 µT). The 3.5 ppm pool is 73.5-220.5 Hz from water - safely outside direct-sat. No masking; the issue is pool degeneracy with APT, not water saturation.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: The amide group's kex=65.5/s and shift=3.5 ppm are class-level amide values borrowed from brain/human APT measurements - NOT glutamine's own primary amide and NOT liver. The in-vivo observed shift, if the primary amide is ~2 ppm, differs from the 3.5 ppm simulated. Confidence is low; the whole simulated glutamine contrast inherits the wrong shift and a borrowed kex. The amine group is unknown (not simulated).

You would need multi-B1 AREX or omega-plot AND an independent constraint (e.g. MRS concentration) to attribute any 3.5 ppm amplitude to glutamine - and even then the borrowed primary-amide shift (3.5 vs true ~2 ppm) breaks the assumption. Realistically glutamine is not independently quantifiable by CEST in this run; a 2 ppm MTRasym would be a re-simulation, not this run's result.

Caveats / critique (9 points, 379 words) — 30 mM (range 20-50 mM) glutamine is reasonable - MRS (PMID 11859290, 17128381) shows Gln as a detectable but minor liver peak. Defensible, but at 30 mM the CEST…
  • 30 mM (range 20-50 mM) glutamine is reasonable - MRS (PMID 11859290, 17128381) shows Gln as a detectable but minor liver peak. Defensible, but at 30 mM the CEST contrast is intrinsically small (simulated max 0.3-1.9% across fields).
  • Serious shift discrepancy: the chemist estimated the side-chain PRIMARY amide near 2.0 ppm, but the simulation FORCED it to the class-level amide shift of 3.5 ppm (median of 16 backbone-amide/brain/liver APT values). A primary amide (R-CONH2) resonates distinctly upfield of the backbone amide (~3.5 ppm), closer to ~2 ppm as the chemist said.
  • So glutamine's peak was placed at EXACTLY 3.5 ppm, creating an artificial 0.0 Hz degeneracy with the protein APT pool - glutamine was simulated with backbone-amide physics, not primary-amide physics. The amine NH3+ (2.8 ppm) is NOT SIMULATED - UNKNOWN (no reference amine value), fast, baseline-buried. Carboxyl (0 H) correctly gives no CEST.
  • The simulation used 3.5 ppm (class-level amide) for the glutamine side-chain primary amide, but a primary amide is expected near ~2 ppm (the chemist's own estimate) and is upfield of the backbone APT.
  • No in-vivo measurement of the glutamine primary amide exists in the reference table - the 3.5 ppm is the APT class value, likely the wrong offset for a primary amide.
  • None omitted, but the class-level amide shift assigned to the side-chain PRIMARY amide (3.5 ppm) is arguably a mis-classification of the offset: a primary amide is a distinct exchangeable group that should not be folded into the 3.5 ppm backbone-amide peak.

In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — axial, centred at the level of the kidneys (just below the liver dome, at the renal hilum)

Why this scan: An axial slice at the kidney-liver window contains liver, renal cortex and renal medulla in one FOV. These tissues have sharply different glycogen, amide (protein) and glutamine content, while their MT/NOE backgrounds are similar. If a Z-offset dip tracks the known organ concentration ranking (e.g. cortex > medulla for amide), it is metabolite-specific exchange, not generic MT. One compromise saturation is applied to all ROIs, mirroring the simulation's with-vs-without logic.

ROIWhere it is drawnRole
liver target tissueRight hepatic lobe anterior segment, at least 2 cm from the diaphragm and capsule, avoiding vessels; ~1.5 cm2.target tissue; high glycogen and protein/amide
renal cortexOuter renal cortex of the left kidney, mid-parenchyma, away from pyramids and renal pelvis; ~1 cm2.comparison; high protein/amide, low glycogen
renal medullaRenal pyramids (medulla) of the left kidney, central region; ~0.6 cm2.comparison; low protein, higher water content, different amide/glycogen
spleenMid-spleen parenchyma, anterior-posterior midplane, avoiding capsule; ~1 cm2.comparison; protein-rich, low glycogen, different from liver
paraspinal muscleRight quadratus lumborum/erector spinae at the level of the kidneys; ~1 cm2.comparison; high protein, very low glycogen, near-zero glutamine

Scan protocol: 3 T, pulsed rectangular train (duty-cycled, SAR-limited at 3 T), B1=0.5 µT, 10 pulses × 100 ms (interpulse delay 100 ms, duty cycle 50%), total Tsat=1900 ms, TR=2100 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): 10 pulses x 100 ms on = 1000 ms plus 9×100 ms off = 900 ms = 1900 ms total saturation; duty = 100/(100+100) = 50%. The 1900 ms saturation block plus a ~150 ms single-shot radial readout fits inside TR=2100 ms. Mean B1 0.5 µT at 50% duty over an 80 mm hepatic/renal slab is within 3 T body-coil SAR limits.

Compromise rationale:

  • Physicist recommended 0.75 µT for the amide pool, 0.25 µT for glycogen, 0.5 µT for glutamine, all at 3000 ms. A single 0.5 µT, 50% duty train keeps the B1 near the amide/glutamine optimum; the 1900 ms on+off train gives ~1000 ms effective saturation, under-saturating all three versus the simulated 3000 ms, but glycogen (rNOE, non-exchangeable) is most robust.
  • The amide pool, the highest-simulated-contrast candidate (~4.4% at 3T), is the priority and is best covered by this B1; the shorter Tsat is an accepted trade-off for SAR and the TR budget.

Fat suppression: SPIR (spectral-spatial inversion recovery) prepulse before the CEST slab, plus water-selective excitation of the readout. The upper-abdominal slice at the renal hilum abuts hepatic capsule fat and perinephric/visceral fat; without fat suppression the fat peaks at ~1 and ~-1 ppm would swamp the glycogen glycoNOE peaks.

Motion mitigation: Self-navigated radial (GRASP/golden-angle) readout plus respiratory navigator gating; free-breathing to avoid breath-hold variability that would change hepatic glycogen. Practical constraint: ~3-4 min per Z-offset stack; whole Z-spectrum (12 offsets) ~1 h. No cardiac gating needed (off-heart).

Slice coverage: Single axial slab, 80 mm thick, centred at the renal hilum level (mid-kidney, just inferior to the liver dome), covering liver, both kidneys (cortex+medulla), spleen and paraspinal muscle. FOV 320×256 mm, matrix 96×96, pixel ~3.3×2.7 mm.

Structures in FOV: liver, left kidney (renal cortex, renal medulla), spleen, right paraspinal muscle (quadratus lumborum/erector spinae), aorta, inferior vena cava

Z-spectrum sampling offsets:

  • -8.00 ppm: far-off baseline reference
  • -3.50 ppm: Mobile protein/peptide amide pool (rNOE/mirror), symmetric reference
  • -2.80 ppm: L-Glutamine amine symmetric reference
  • -2.00 ppm: L-Glutamine symmetric reference
  • -1.60 ppm: Glycogen aliphatic rNOE upfield tail
  • -1.00 ppm: Glycogen glycoNOE primary peak
  • +0.00 ppm: water (0 ppm), WASSR B0 reference
  • +1.00 ppm: Glycogen glycosyl hydroxyl (secondary)
  • +2.00 ppm: L-Glutamine side-chain primary amide
  • +2.80 ppm: L-Glutamine alpha-amine (secondary)
  • +3.50 ppm: Mobile protein/peptide amide pool (APT positive)
  • +8.00 ppm: far-off baseline reference

Differential analysis plan:

  • For each offset, compute per-ROI MTRasym = [S(-d) - S(+d)] / S0 (WASSR-corrected) at 3.5, -1.0, -1.6 and 2.0 ppm, and a Lorentzian difference to remove the broad MT/NOE background.
  • A metabolite is supported if the ROI-to-ROI dip pattern tracks the concentration ranking: amide (3.5 ppm) should follow cortex >= liver > spleen > medulla with a muscle dip of comparable size (confirms a protein pool)
  • glycogen (-1.0/-1.6 ppm) should follow liver >> kidney > spleen/muscle ~0 (confirms a liver-specific glycogen store, distinguishing it from the generic rNOE which would be roughly equal across ROIs) glutamine (2.0 ppm) should be small and roughly similar across liver/kidney with low spleen/muscle. If all ROIs show the same dip at an offset, it is background MT/NOE, not that metabolite.

Not actively targeted: L-Glutamate and L-Alanine were not actively designed around: the physicist reported no detectable simulated CEST contrast for them at any field strength, and their 1H shifts/amine pools are not well-separated enough at 3 T to add a dedicated offset within this scan's budget.

Caveats:

  • The renal medulla ROI is small (~0.6 cm2) and partial-volume with cortex/pyramids limits precision. B0/B1 inhomogeneity across a 320 mm abdominal slab persists after WASSR/Dixon; the pipeline's 0.7x-1.3x B1 re-simulation bounds this. Susceptibility from the liver-dome-diaphragm and bowel gas distorts the Z-spectrum near the FOV edges.
  • One compromise B1/Tsat (0.5 µT, 50% duty, 1900 ms) cannot be simultaneously optimal for amide (0.75 µT preferred), glycogen (0.25 µT) and glutamine; the duty-cycled Tsat under-saturates all three versus the simulated 3000 ms, so absolute contrast will be lower than the physicist's 3 T figures.
  • Most comparison-tissue concentrations are estimates without direct citations, so the concentration ranking, not the absolute values, carries the discriminating evidence.
